claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Clark et al., 1991; Kumar et al., 2000; Parham, 2001; Sebire and Malone, 2003.

claims.claim: MRFs are used in the clinical diagnosis of RMS.
claims.source: These tumors express myogenic regulatory transcription factors (MRFs) including Myogenic factor 5 (MYF5) and Myoblast determination protein D (MYOD) (Clark et al., 1991; Kumar et al., 2000; Parham, 2001; Sebire and Malone, 2003) and are used in the clinical diagnosis of RMS.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Clark et al., 1991; Kumar et al., 2000; Parham, 2001; Sebire and Malone, 2003.

claims.claim: Alveolar RMS (ARMS) harbor Pax7-FOXO and Pax3-FOXO genomic fusions.
claims.source: Alveolar RMS (ARMS) harbor Pax7-FOXO and Pax3-FOXO genomic fusions (Sorensen et al., 2002) and have few additional recurrent genomic changes (Chen et al., 2013b; Shern et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Sorensen et al., 2002; Chen et al., 2013b; Shern et al., 2014.

claims.claim: ARMS have few additional recurrent genomic changes beyond PAX-FOXO fusions.
claims.source: Alveolar RMS (ARMS) harbor Pax7-FOXO and Pax3-FOXO genomic fusions (Sorensen et al., 2002) and have few additional recurrent genomic changes (Chen et al., 2013b; Shern et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2013b; Shern et al., 2014.

claims.claim: 90% of human embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (ERMS) have RAS pathway activation.
claims.source: By contrast, 90% of human embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (ERMS) have RAS pathway activation and a higher mutation burden when compared with ARMS (Chen et al., 2013b; Langenau et al., 2007; Shern et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2013b; Langenau et al., 2007; Shern et al., 2014.

claims.claim: ERMS have a higher mutation burden when compared with ARMS.
claims.source: By contrast, 90% of human embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (ERMS) have RAS pathway activation and a higher mutation burden when compared with ARMS (Chen et al., 2013b; Langenau et al., 2007; Shern et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2013b; Langenau et al., 2007; Shern et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Common mutations found in ERMS include inactivation of Tp53.
claims.source: Common mutations found in ERMS include inactivation of Tp53 and activating mutations of FGFR4, PDGFA, and NOTCH1 (Chen et al., 2013b; Shern et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2013b; Shern et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Common mutations found in ERMS include activating mutations of FGFR4, PDGFA, and NOTCH1.
claims.source: Common mutations found in ERMS include inactivation of Tp53 and activating mutations of FGFR4, PDGFA, and NOTCH1 (Chen et al., 2013b; Shern et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2013b; Shern et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The Sonic-Hedgehog signaling pathway has been shown to regulate TPC function in a subset of human RMS.
claims.source: In fact, to date, only the Sonic-Hedgehog and canonical WNT/B-catenin signaling pathways have been shown to regulate TPC function in a subset of human RMS (Chen et al., 2014; Satheesha et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2014; Satheesha et al., 2016.

claims.claim: The canonical WNT/B-catenin signaling pathway has been shown to regulate TPC function in a subset of human RMS.
claims.source: In fact, to date, only the Sonic-Hedgehog and canonical WNT/B-catenin signaling pathways have been shown to regulate TPC function in a subset of human RMS (Chen et al., 2014; Satheesha et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2014; Satheesha et al., 2016.

claims.claim: MYF5 and MYOD are highly expressed in human and animal models of RMS.
claims.source: Despite MYF5 and MYOD being highly expressed in human and animal models of RMS (Langenau et al., 2007; Rubin et al., 2011), exerting important roles in muscle development and stem cell self-renewal in regeneration (Buckingham and Rigby, 2014), and being able to reprogram fibroblasts into proliferating myoblasts (Braun et al., 1989; Tapscott et al., 1988); a functional requirement for these transcription factors in regulating RMS growth has gone unexplored since their discovery over two decades ago.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Langenau et al., 2007; Rubin et al., 2011.

claims.claim: MYF5 and MYOD exert important roles in muscle development and stem cell self-renewal in regeneration.
claims.source: Despite MYF5 and MYOD being highly expressed in human and animal models of RMS (Langenau et al., 2007; Rubin et al., 2011), exerting important roles in muscle development and stem cell self-renewal in regeneration (Buckingham and Rigby, 2014), and being able to reprogram fibroblasts into proliferating myoblasts (Braun et al., 1989; Tapscott et al., 1988); a functional requirement for these transcription factors in regulating RMS growth has gone unexplored since their discovery over two decades ago.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Buckingham and Rigby, 2014.

claims.claim: MYF5 and MYOD are able to reprogram fibroblasts into proliferating myoblasts.
claims.source: Despite MYF5 and MYOD being highly expressed in human and animal models of RMS (Langenau et al., 2007; Rubin et al., 2011), exerting important roles in muscle development and stem cell self-renewal in regeneration (Buckingham and Rigby, 2014), and being able to reprogram fibroblasts into proliferating myoblasts (Braun et al., 1989; Tapscott et al., 1988); a functional requirement for these transcription factors in regulating RMS growth has gone unexplored since their discovery over two decades ago.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Braun et al., 1989; Tapscott et al., 1988.

claims.claim: A functional requirement for MYF5 and MYOD in regulating RMS growth has gone unexplored since their discovery over two decades ago.
claims.source: Despite MYF5 and MYOD being highly expressed in human and animal models of RMS (Langenau et al., 2007; Rubin et al., 2011), exerting important roles in muscle development and stem cell self-renewal in regeneration (Buckingham and Rigby, 2014), and being able to reprogram fibroblasts into proliferating myoblasts (Braun et al., 1989; Tapscott et al., 1988); a functional requirement for these transcription factors in regulating RMS growth has gone unexplored since their discovery over two decades ago.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this work.

claims.claim: Transgenic zebrafish models have become a powerful tool to uncover new biological insights into human cancer.
claims.source: Transgenic zebrafish models have become a powerful tool to uncover new biological insights into human cancer (Langenau et al., 2003, 2007; Le et al., 2007; Park et al., 2008; Patton et al., 2005; Sabaawy et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2004; Zhuravleva et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claims.claim: A mosaic transgenic zebrafish expressing human kRASG12D under control of the rag2 minimal promoter has been developed for ERMS.
claims.source: In the setting of ERMS, we have developed a mosaic transgenic zebrafish that express human kRASG12D under control of the rag2 minimal promoter, which is expressed in lymphoid cells (Jessen et al., 2001; Langenau et al., 2003) and muscle progenitor cells (Langenau et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Jessen et al., 2001; Langenau et al., 2003; Langenau et al., 2007.

claims.claim: The rag2 minimal promoter is expressed in lymphoid cells.
claims.source: In the setting of ERMS, we have developed a mosaic transgenic zebrafish that express human kRASG12D under control of the rag2 minimal promoter, which is expressed in lymphoid cells (Jessen et al., 2001; Langenau et al., 2003) and muscle progenitor cells (Langenau et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Jessen et al., 2001; Langenau et al., 2003.

claims.claim: The rag2 minimal promoter is expressed in muscle progenitor cells.
claims.source: In the setting of ERMS, we have developed a mosaic transgenic zebrafish that express human kRASG12D under control of the rag2 minimal promoter, which is expressed in lymphoid cells (Jessen et al., 2001; Langenau et al., 2003) and muscle progenitor cells (Langenau et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Langenau et al., 2007.

claims.claim: 20–40% of mosaic injected fish expressing kRASG12D under the rag2 promoter developed ERMS.
claims.source: Thus, when kRASG12D was expressed under control of this promoter, 20–40% mosaic injected fish developed ERMS (Langenau et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Langenau et al., 2007.

claims.claim: 10–20 transgene copies are commonly integrated into the zebrafish genome in mosaic transgenesis.
claims.source: Because 10–20 transgene copies are commonly integrated into the genome (Langenau et al., 2008), one can inject multiple transgenes into one-cell stage embryos with stable integration and expression being observed in developing tumors.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Langenau et al., 2008.

claims.claim: The zebrafish ERMS model accurately mimics many of the molecular underpinnings of the human disease.
claims.source: Importantly, the zebrafish model accurately mimics many of the molecular underpinnings of the human disease and has been used to uncover important genes and pathways relevant to human cancer (Chen et al., 2013a, 2014; Ignatius et al., 2012; Langenau et al., 2007; Le et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2013a, 2014; Ignatius et al., 2012; Langenau et al., 2007; Le et al., 2013.

claims.claim: The zebrafish model has been used to identify functional heterogeneity in molecularly defined cell types, including isolation of myf5:GFP+ TPCs.
claims.source: The model has also been used to identify functional heterogeneity in molecularly defined cell types, including isolation of myf5:GFP+ TPCs (Ignatius et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Ignatius et al., 2012.

claims.claim: myf5 is highly expressed in undifferentiated, molecularly defined TPCs in zebrafish kRASG12D-induced ERMS.
claims.source: We have uncovered that myf5 is highly expressed in undifferentiated, molecularly defined TPCs in zebrafish kRASG12D-induced ERMS (Langenau et al., 2007; Ignatius et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Langenau et al., 2007; Ignatius et al., 2012.

claims.claim: The TPC fraction in zebrafish ERMS shares molecular and functional properties with non-transformed muscle satellite stem cells.
claims.source: Remarkably, this TPC fraction shares molecular and functional properties with non-transformed muscle satellite stem cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data and citations in the manuscript.

claims.claim: myf5:GFP+/myosin-negative progenitor cells drive tumor growth in the zebrafish ERMS model.
claims.source: For example, cell transplantation and direct live cell imaging has revealed that myf5:GFP+/myosin-negative progenitor cells drive tumor growth and specifically label TPCs in this animal model (Ignatius et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Ignatius et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2014.

claims.claim: myf5:GFP+/myosin-negative progenitor cells specifically label TPCs in the zebrafish ERMS model.
claims.source: For example, cell transplantation and direct live cell imaging has revealed that myf5:GFP+/myosin-negative progenitor cells drive tumor growth and specifically label TPCs in this animal model (Ignatius et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Ignatius et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The mylpfa promoter faithfully drives expression in terminally-differentiated muscle cells in both transient and stable transgenic fish.
claims.source: This transgene faithfully drives expression in terminally-differentiated muscle cells in both transient and stable transgenic fish (Xu et al., 1999; Langenau et al., 2007; Ignatius et al., 2012; Storer et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2014) and has been used to identify zebrafish ERMS cell subfractions that lack myf5, have low proliferative capacity, cannot self-renew, and do not sustain ERMS growth in vivo (Ignatius et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Xu et al., 1999; Langenau et al., 2007; Ignatius et al., 2012; Storer et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Primary kRASG12D-induced ERMS were comprised of 50% undifferentiated stage 1 ERMS.
claims.source: As reported previously, primary kRASG12D-induced ERMS were comprised of 50% undifferentiated stage 1 ERMS (N = 5 of 10, Figure 1B,C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2), which harbored mostly small round blue cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 1B,C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: mylpfa:myf5 expressing primary ERMS contained only 7.7% stage 1 ERMS.
claims.source: By contrast, mylpfa:myf5 expressing primary ERMS contained only 7.7% stage 1 ERMS (N = 2 of 26, p=0.015, Chi-square test, Figure 1E–F), with the remaining tumors being highly differentiated stage 2 and 3 ERMS (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 1E–F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: mylpfa:myf5 expressing ERMS cells had high myf5 transgene expression.
claims.source: Transcriptional profiling of bulk tumor cells by qRT-PCR confirmed that mylpfa:myf5 expressing ERMS cells had high myf5 transgene expression, were more differentiated, and yet also had elevated expression of TPC-associated markers including c-met and cadherin 15 (Figure 1G, Langenau et al., 2007; Ignatius et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: mylpfa:myf5 expressing ERMS cells were more differentiated.
claims.source: Transcriptional profiling of bulk tumor cells by qRT-PCR confirmed that mylpfa:myf5 expressing ERMS cells had high myf5 transgene expression, were more differentiated, and yet also had elevated expression of TPC-associated markers including c-met and cadherin 15 (Figure 1G, Langenau et al., 2007; Ignatius et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: mylpfa:myf5 expressing ERMS cells had elevated expression of TPC-associated markers including c-met and cadherin 15.
claims.source: Transcriptional profiling of bulk tumor cells by qRT-PCR confirmed that mylpfa:myf5 expressing ERMS cells had high myf5 transgene expression, were more differentiated, and yet also had elevated expression of TPC-associated markers including c-met and cadherin 15 (Figure 1G, Langenau et al., 2007; Ignatius et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1G and citations to Langenau et al., 2007; Ignatius et al., 2012.

claims.claim: c-met and cadherin 15 are commonly expressed in zebrafish muscle progenitor and satellite cells.
claims.source: These gene markers are also commonly expressed in zebrafish muscle progenitor and satellite cells (Siegel et al., 2013; Gurevich et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Siegel et al., 2013; Gurevich et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Tumors arising in double transgenic rag2:kRASG12D; mylpfa:myf5 expressing ERMS were larger by 30 days postfertilization than those that expressed only kRASG12D.
claims.source: Tumors arising in double transgenic rag2:kRASG12D; mylpfa:myf5 expressing ERMS were also larger by 30 days postfertilization than those that expressed only kRASG12D (Figure 1H, p=0.0108, Student's t-test).
claims.evidence: This is supported by tumor size quantification shown in Figure 1H.

claims.claim: Apoptosis was not altered following re-expression of myf5 in zebrafish ERMS.
claims.source: However, apoptosis was not altered following re-expression of myf5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cleaved caspase-3 staining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: kRASG12D-expressing ERMS were comprised exclusively of undifferentiated stage one tumors following transplantation into immune-deficient rag2E450fs recipient fish.
claims.source: kRASG12D-expressing ERMS were comprised exclusively of undifferentiated stage one tumors (Figure 2B,C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, n=10 transplanted fish arising from four independent tumors).
claims.evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2B,C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: ERMS that re-expressed myf5 had differentiated histology and were comprised exclusively of stage 2 and 3 tumors following transplantation.
claims.source: By contrast, ERMS that re-expressed myf5 had differentiated histology and were comprised exclusively of stage 2 and 3 tumors (Figure 2E,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, n=15 transplanted fish from four independent tumors, p<,0.001, Chi-square test).
claims.evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2E,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Differentiated, mylpfa:mCherry-positive (R+) tumor cells were greatly expanded in ERMS that aberrantly express myf5.
claims.source: Consistent with our histological evaluation, flow cytometric analysis revealed that differentiated, mylpfa:mCherry-positive (R+) tumor cells were greatly expanded in ERMS that aberrantly express myf5 (Figure 2G–I, p=0.006, Student's t-test).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2G–I.

claims.claim: Only the myf5:GFP+ (G+) single-positive ERMS cells from kRASG12D-alone expressing ERMS could efficiently engraft tumors into CG1-strain syngeneic recipient animals.
claims.source: As previously reported (Ignatius et al., 2012), only the myf5:GFP+ (G+) single-positive ERMS cells from kRASG12D-alone expressing ERMS could efficiently engraft tumors into CG1-strain syngeneic recipient animals (Figure 3J and Table 1; N = 3 independent tumors).
claims.evidence: This is supported by limiting dilution transplantation data shown in Figure 3J and Table 1, and citation to Ignatius et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Both the myf5:GFP+ single-positive (G+) and differentiated myf5:GFP+; mylpfa:mCherry+ double positive (G+R+) ERMS cells could engraft disease when isolated from mylpfa:myf5 expressing ERMS.
claims.source: By contrast, both the myf5:GFP+ single-positive (G+) and differentiated myf5:GFP+; mylpfa:mCherry+ double positive (G+R+) ERMS cells could engraft disease when isolated from mylpfa:myf5 expressing ERMS (N = 3 tumors analyzed, Table 1 and Figure 3L; p=0.0002, ELDA analysis).
claims.evidence: This is supported by limiting dilution transplantation data shown in Table 1 and Figure 3L.

claims.claim: MYOD and MYF5 were expressed along with specific muscle genes and defined two distinct gene regulatory modules in human RMS.
claims.source: Analysis of microarray gene expression (N = 133 samples) (Davicioni et al., 2009) and RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) data sets (N = 98 samples) (Shern et al., 2014) uncovered that MYOD and MYF5 were expressed along with specific muscle genes and defined two distinct gene regulatory modules in human RMS.
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of microarray and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4A,B and citations to Davicioni et al., 2009; Shern et al., 2014.

claims.claim: One gene module in human RMS included the co-expression of MYF5, MYF6 and PAX7.
claims.source: One gene module included the co-expression of MYF5, MYF6 and PAX7 while the other expressed MYOD and higher levels of CDH15, and MYOG (Figure 4A,B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4A,B.

claims.claim: One gene module in human RMS expressed MYOD and higher levels of CDH15, and MYOG.
claims.source: One gene module included the co-expression of MYF5, MYF6 and PAX7 while the other expressed MYOD and higher levels of CDH15, and MYOG (Figure 4A,B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4A,B.

claims.claim: The expression of MYF5 and MYOD proteins was largely mutually exclusive in human RMS cell lines.
claims.source: Remarkably, we found that the expression of these proteins was largely mutually exclusive in human RMS cell lines (N = 7, Figure 4C), suggesting that these proteins may act redundantly to regulate human RMS growth.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Only the Rh18 ERMS cells expressed MYF5 in the panel of human cell lines analyzed.
claims.source: This analysis also uncovered that only the Rh18 ERMS cells expressed MYF5 in our panel of human cell lines.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: MYF5 and MYOD were mutually exclusively expressed in Rh18 and RD cells at the single cell level.
claims.source: MYF5 and MYOD expression were also assessed at the single cell level through immunofluorescence and verified that MYF5 and MYOD were mutually exclusively expressed in Rh18 and RD cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: si-MYF5 treated Rh18 cells showed a 70% reduction in S-phase cycling cells following 48 hr of treatment.
claims.source: For example, si-MYF5 treated cells showed a remarkable 70% reduction in S-phase cycling cells following 48 hr of treatment (p<0.001, Student's t-test, Figure 4E–F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by EdU/PI flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4E–F.

claims.claim: All sh-MYF5 knockdown Rh18 cells showed a remarkable cell cycle arrest with a virtual abrogation of S-phase cycling cells.
claims.source: All sh-MYF5 knockdown cells showed a remarkable cell cycle arrest with a virtual abrogation of S-phase cycling cells (Figure 4H–I and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A; p<0.001, Student's t-test).
claims.evidence: This is supported by EdU/PI flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4H–I and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: sh-MYF5 knockdown in Rh18 cells led to a significant 60% decrease in cell number as assessed by manual nuclei counts performed at 96 hr.
claims.source: This phenotype was not associated with an overall increase in apoptosis (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C,D) and yet lead to a significant 60% decrease in cell number as assessed by manual nuclei counts performed at 96 hr and compared with shRNA control treated cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 3E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by nuclei count data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3E.

claims.claim: siRNA knockdown of MYOD in RD cells resulted in reduced proliferation and a striking reduction in S-phase cycling cells.
claims.source: siRNA knockdown resulted in reduced proliferation and a striking reduction in S-phase cycling cells (Figure 4J–O; p<0.001, Student's t-test).
claims.evidence: This is supported by EdU/PI flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4J–O.

claims.claim: RD cell number was reduced >30% following stable sh-MYOD knockdown.
claims.source: In fact, RD cell number was reduced >30% following stable sh-MYOD knockdown (Figure 4—figure supplement 3H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by nuclei count data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3H.

claims.claim: Sphere colony formation was greatly reduced in RD cells following shRNA knockdown of MYOD.
claims.source: In support of MYOD having important roles in regulating TPC number, sphere colony formation was also greatly reduced in RD cells following shRNA knockdown (p<0.01, Figure 4—figure supplement 3I,J).
claims.evidence: This is supported by sphere colony formation assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3I,J.

claims.claim: MYOD knockdown impaired cell cycle and growth in ERMS cell lines 381T and RMS559 and the ARMS cell line Rh3.
claims.source: Finally, MYOD knockdown also impaired cell cycle and growth in additional RMS cell lines including ERMS cell lines 381T and RMS559 and the ARMS cell line Rh3. These cells lines all had significant reductions in S-phase cycling cells following siRNA treatment with variable effects on apoptosis at the time points analyzed (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A–L).
claims.evidence: This is supported by EdU/PI flow cytometry and apoptosis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A–L.

claims.claim: Tumor volume was reduced in MYF5 knockdown Rh18 cells in xenograft experiments while control cells continued to grow.
claims.source: Serial bioluminescence imaging showed that tumor volume was reduced in MYF5 knockdown cells while control cells continued to grow (p<0.05, Student's t-test; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by bioluminescence imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: MYF5 knockdown Rh18 cells were largely undetected at late time points in xenograft experiments.
claims.source: MYF5 knockdown cells were largely undetected at late time points (p<0.05, Student's t-Test; Figure 5B,C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by bioluminescence imaging data shown in Figure 5B,C.

claims.claim: Only 2 of 12 mice had tumors derived from MYF5-deficient Rh18 cells at necropsy.
claims.source: Analysis of mice at necropsy revealed that only 2 of 12 mice had tumors derived from MYF5-deficient Rh18 cells and that overall tumor weight was greatly reduced when compared with control Rh18 knockdown cells (p<0.01; Student's t-test; Figure 5D–E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by necropsy data shown in Figure 5D–E.

claims.claim: Overall tumor weight was greatly reduced in MYF5 knockdown Rh18 xenografts when compared with control Rh18 knockdown cells.
claims.source: Analysis of mice at necropsy revealed that only 2 of 12 mice had tumors derived from MYF5-deficient Rh18 cells and that overall tumor weight was greatly reduced when compared with control Rh18 knockdown cells (p<0.01; Student's t-test; Figure 5D–E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by necropsy data shown in Figure 5D–E.

claims.claim: shRNA knockdown of MYOD resulted in reduced xenograft growth of both RD and RMS559 cells when assessed by total body luciferase imaging completed overtime.
claims.source: Using the same approach outlined above, we found that shRNA knockdown of MYOD resulted in efficient knockdown prior to tumor cell implantation (Figure 5F,K) and reduced xenograft growth of both RD and RMS559 cells when assessed by total body luciferase imaging completed overtime (p<0.01; Figure 5F–H,K–M and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by bioluminescence imaging data shown in Figure 5F–H,K–M and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C.

claims.claim: MYOD knockdown tumors were smaller at the time of necropsy and weighed significantly less than control shRNA expressing tumors.
claims.source: MYOD knockdown tumors were also smaller at the time of necropsy (Figure 5I,N) and weighed significantly less than control shRNA expressing tumors (p<0.01, Student's t-test; Figure 5J,O).
claims.evidence: This is supported by necropsy data shown in Figure 5I,J,N,O.

claims.claim: 86% of commonly bound genomic DNA regions by MYOD and MYF5 were confined to enhancer regions as defined by H3K27-acetylation occupancy.
claims.source: 86% of commonly bound genomic DNA regions were confined to enhancer regions as defined by H3K27-acetylation occupancy (Figure 6A,B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 6A,B.

claims.claim: Unbiased analysis of commonly bound target genes by MYF5 and MYOD revealed an enrichment of genes that regulate cell cycle and myogenic cell fate.
claims.source: Unbiased analysis of commonly bound target genes using GREAT (McLean et al., 2010), Supplementary file 2) revealed an enrichment of genes that regulate cell cycle and myogenic cell fate (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GREAT analysis shown in Figure 6C and Supplementary file 2.

claims.claim: Both Myogenin and CDH15 were downregulated following MYF5 or MYOD knockdown at either 48 or 72 hr.
claims.source: As expected if myogenic transcription factors regulate muscle cell fate, both Myogenin and CDH15 were downregulated following MYF5 or MYOD knockdown at either 48 or 72 hr (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: CCND2 was reduced following MYF5 or MYOD knockdown.
claims.source: Additionally, the cell cycle regulatory gene, CCND2 was also reduced following MYF5 or MYOD knockdown (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: The zebrafish orthologue ccnd2a transcript showed a trend toward higher expression in mylpfa:myf5 expressing zebrafish ERMS.
claims.source: Moreover, the zebrafish orthologue ccnd2a transcript showed a trend toward higher expression in mylpfa:myf5 expressing zebrafish ERMS (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), correlating well with elevated myf5 expression in these tumors.
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: CCND2 is amplified in a subset of human RMS.
claims.source: CCND2 is a CDK4/6-associated cyclin that is amplified in a subset of human RMS and is required for cell proliferation and viability in human RMS (Chen et al., 2013a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2013a.

claims.claim: CCND2 is required for cell proliferation and viability in human RMS.
claims.source: CCND2 is a CDK4/6-associated cyclin that is amplified in a subset of human RMS and is required for cell proliferation and viability in human RMS (Chen et al., 2013a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2013a.

claims.claim: CCND2 is a predicted direct target of MYF5 and MYOD binding.
claims.source: Importantly, CCND2 is a predicted direct target of MYF5 and MYOD binding (Conerly et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Conerly et al., 2016.

claims.claim: MYF5 and MYOD act redundantly in muscle development to regulate muscle specification and differentiation.
claims.source: For example, MYF5 and MYOD are well-known to act redundantly in muscle development to regulate muscle specification and differentiation (Rudnicki et al., 1993).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Rudnicki et al., 1993.

claims.claim: Redundancy of Myf5 and MyoD in development and muscle injury has been reported in zebrafish.
claims.source: This same redundancy of Myf5 and MyoD in development and muscle injury has now been reported in zebrafish (Hinits et al., 2009; Siegel et al., 2013), Drosophila (Abmayr and Keller, 1998) and Xenopus (Chanoine and Hardy, 2003), showing a high conservation of the MYOD/MYF5 transcriptional machinery in regulating muscle specification and development throughout evolution.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Hinits et al., 2009; Siegel et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Redundancy of Myf5 and MyoD in development and muscle injury has been reported in Drosophila.
claims.source: This same redundancy of Myf5 and MyoD in development and muscle injury has now been reported in zebrafish (Hinits et al., 2009; Siegel et al., 2013), Drosophila (Abmayr and Keller, 1998) and Xenopus (Chanoine and Hardy, 2003), showing a high conservation of the MYOD/MYF5 transcriptional machinery in regulating muscle specification and development throughout evolution.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Abmayr and Keller, 1998.

claims.claim: Redundancy of Myf5 and MyoD in development and muscle injury has been reported in Xenopus.
claims.source: This same redundancy of Myf5 and MyoD in development and muscle injury has now been reported in zebrafish (Hinits et al., 2009; Siegel et al., 2013), Drosophila (Abmayr and Keller, 1998) and Xenopus (Chanoine and Hardy, 2003), showing a high conservation of the MYOD/MYF5 transcriptional machinery in regulating muscle specification and development throughout evolution.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Chanoine and Hardy, 2003.

claims.claim: MRFs are required for self-renewal of adult muscle satellite cells.
claims.source: These same MRFs are also required for self-renewal of adult muscle satellite cells (Cooper et al., 1999; Ustanina et al., 2007; Yablonka-Reuveni et al., 1999), yet roles for these factors in individually regulating muscle fate and self-renewal are now just emerging in the literature.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Cooper et al., 1999; Ustanina et al., 2007; Yablonka-Reuveni et al., 1999.

claims.claim: A subset of muscle progenitors are specified by MYOD without the contribution of MYF5.
claims.source: For example, a subset of muscle progenitors are specified by MYOD without the contribution of MYF5 (Haldar et al., 2008, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Haldar et al., 2008, 2014.

claims.claim: A subset of adult muscle progenitors express MYF5 and then MYOD sequentially during their specification with both being required for muscle regeneration following injury.
claims.source: Moreover, a subset of adult muscle progenitors express MYF5 and then MYOD sequentially during their specification with both being required for muscle regeneration following injury (Comai et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Comai et al., 2014.

claims.claim: m-cadherin (CDH15) and myogenin (MYOG) were transcriptionally regulated by MYF5 and MYOD in human RMS.
claims.source: For example, m-cadherin (CDH15) and myogenin (MYOG) were transcriptionally regulated by MYF5 and MYOD in human RMS, consistent with regulation of these same factors by MYF5 and MYOD in myoblasts (Conerly et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 6E and citation to Conerly et al., 2016.

claims.claim: The CDK4/6-associated cyclin D2 (CCND2) complex is required for myoblast proliferation.
claims.source: Importantly, the CDK4/6-associated cyclin D2 (CCND2) complex is required for both myoblast proliferation and human RMS growth, is highly expressed in primary human RMS and is amplified in a subset of human and zebrafish RMS (Chen et al., 2013a; Saab et al., 2006; Webster and Fan, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2013a; Saab et al., 2006; Webster and Fan, 2013.

claims.claim: The CDK4/6-associated cyclin D2 (CCND2) complex is highly expressed in primary human RMS.
claims.source: Importantly, the CDK4/6-associated cyclin D2 (CCND2) complex is required for both myoblast proliferation and human RMS growth, is highly expressed in primary human RMS and is amplified in a subset of human and zebrafish RMS (Chen et al., 2013a; Saab et al., 2006; Webster and Fan, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2013a; Saab et al., 2006; Webster and Fan, 2013.

results.result: RMS is a pediatric muscle malignancy characterized by impaired differentiation and expression of myogenic regulatory transcription factors MYF5 and MYOD, which are used clinically for diagnosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C16, C17, and C18 establish the basic characteristics of RMS. These are well-supported by citations to established literature and represent accepted knowledge in the field. The claims are consistent and mutually reinforcing.

results.result: ARMS and ERMS represent distinct molecular subtypes with different genomic characteristics: ARMS harbor PAX-FOXO fusions with few additional changes, while ERMS have RAS pathway activation, higher mutation burden, and mutations in TP53, FGFR4, PDGFA, and NOTCH1.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C24 describe established molecular differences between RMS subtypes. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to prior genomic studies. This represents background knowledge rather than novel findings from this study.

results.result: Prior to this work, the field consensus was that MRF expression reflected the cell of transformation rather than being required for tumor growth, despite MYF5 and MYOD being highly expressed in RMS models and having known roles in muscle development and cellular reprogramming.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C27-C30 establish the prior state of knowledge and the gap this study addresses. These are well-supported by citations and provide important context for the novelty of the functional studies presented. C30 appropriately frames the research question.

results.result: The zebrafish kRASG12D-induced ERMS model, using the rag2 promoter expressed in lymphoid and muscle progenitor cells, accurately mimics human disease and has been validated for studying RMS biology and identifying TPCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C38 describe the zebrafish model system used in this study. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to prior work establishing and validating this model. This provides essential methodological context.

results.result: In zebrafish ERMS, myf5 is highly expressed in undifferentiated TPCs that share properties with muscle satellite stem cells, with myf5:GFP+/myosin-negative cells specifically labeling and driving tumor growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C43 establish prior characterization of the zebrafish model relevant to this study. These are supported by citations to previous work and provide the foundation for the myf5 overexpression experiments. The mylpfa promoter specificity (C43) is well-documented.

results.result: Re-expression of myf5 under the mylpfa promoter in zebrafish ERMS resulted in more differentiated tumors (7.7% vs 50% stage 1), elevated TPC markers (c-met, cadherin 15), larger tumor size at 30 dpf, without changes in apoptosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C51 are supported by histological analysis (Figure 1B-F), qRT-PCR data (Figure 1G), tumor size measurements (Figure 1H), and apoptosis assays (Figure 1—supplement 3). The statistical significance (p=0.015, Chi-square) for differentiation changes is appropriate. However, the proliferation data shows high variability and only a trend (C51, Figure 1—supplement 3D), which appropriately tempers conclusions about mechanism.

results.result: Myf5 expression caused tumors to initiate earlier and have higher penetrance in zebrafish ERMS.
results.evaluation: Claims C5 and C6 are supported by Kaplan-Meier analysis (Figure 1I, p<0.001, log-rank test). The data clearly show accelerated tumor onset and increased penetrance with mylpfa:myf5 expression. Statistical analysis is appropriate.

results.result: Following transplantation into immune-deficient recipients, kRASG12D-alone ERMS remained undifferentiated (stage 1), while mylpfa:myf5 expressing ERMS showed differentiated histology (stage 2-3) with expanded mylpfa:mCherry+ cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54 are supported by histological analysis (Figure 2B-F, p<0.001 Chi-square) and flow cytometry (Figure 2G-I, p=0.006). The transplantation experiments confirm that differentiation effects are maintained in fully transformed cells, strengthening the primary tumor findings.

results.result: Myf5 is sufficient to confer tumor-propagating potential to differentiated ERMS cells: in limiting dilution transplantation, both G+ and G+R+ cells from mylpfa:myf5 ERMS could engraft tumors, while only G+ cells from kRASG12D-alone ERMS were tumorigenic.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C56, and C57 are supported by limiting dilution transplantation data (Figure 3, Table 1, p=0.0002 ELDA analysis). The experiments used appropriate controls, high sort purity (>85%), and multiple independent tumors (N=3). This is a key finding demonstrating that myf5 can reprogram differentiated cells to acquire TPC properties. The ELDA statistical analysis is appropriate for this type of data.

results.result: Analysis of human RMS revealed two distinct gene regulatory modules: one with MYF5, MYF6, and PAX7 co-expression, and another with MYOD and higher CDH15 and MYOG expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C60 are supported by correlation analysis of microarray (N=133) and RNA-seq (N=98) datasets (Figure 4A-B). The analysis appropriately uses Pearson correlation and is consistent across both datasets and RMS subtypes (Figure 4—supplement 1). This establishes inter-tumoral heterogeneity in MRF expression.

results.result: MYF5 and MYOD proteins are mutually exclusively expressed in human RMS cell lines at both bulk and single-cell levels, with only Rh18 cells expressing MYF5 among the panel tested.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C61-C63 are supported by Western blot (Figure 4C, N=7 cell lines) and immunofluorescence (Figure 4—supplement 2). The mutual exclusivity is clearly demonstrated. However, the sample size is limited to 7 cell lines, and only one (Rh18) expresses MYF5, which limits generalizability but is appropriate given the rarity of MYF5-expressing lines.

results.result: MYF5 is required for sustained growth of Rh18 human RMS cells: knockdown resulted in 70% reduction in S-phase cells (siRNA, 48hr) and virtual abrogation of S-phase (shRNA, 72hr), with 60% decrease in cell number without initial apoptosis increase.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C64-C66 are supported by EdU/PI flow cytometry (Figure 4E-I, p<0.001), nuclei counts (Figure 4—supplement 3E), and apoptosis assays (Figure 4—supplement 3B-D). Multiple independent shRNAs (N=3) show consistent effects. The temporal sequence (cell cycle arrest preceding apoptosis) is well-documented. Statistical analysis is appropriate.

results.result: MYOD is required for sustained growth of human RMS cells: knockdown in RD, 381T, RMS559, and Rh3 cells resulted in reduced S-phase cells, decreased cell number (>30% in RD), reduced sphere formation, with variable effects on apoptosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C67-C70 are supported by EdU/PI flow cytometry (Figure 4J-O, Figure 4—supplement 4, p<0.001), nuclei counts (Figure 4—supplement 3H), and sphere assays (Figure 4—supplement 3I-J, p<0.01). Effects are demonstrated across multiple cell lines (RD, 381T, RMS559, Rh3) representing both ERMS and ARMS. Specificity controls (Figure 4—supplement 4M-T) confirm knockdown specificity.

results.result: MYF5 knockdown in Rh18 cells severely impaired xenograft growth: tumor volume was reduced over time, cells were largely undetected at late timepoints, with only 2/12 mice having detectable tumors at necropsy and greatly reduced tumor weight.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C74 are supported by bioluminescence imaging (Figure 5B-C, Figure 5—supplement 1A, p<0.05) and necropsy data (Figure 5D-E, p<0.01). The in vivo requirement for MYF5 is clearly demonstrated. N=6 mice per condition with bilateral implantation (control vs knockdown) provides good experimental design. Rare escaper tumors retained RMS histology (Figure 5—supplement 1D-E).

results.result: MYOD knockdown reduced xenograft growth of RD and RMS559 cells: tumors were smaller and weighed significantly less than controls, though knockdown cells continued to grow at reduced levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C76 are supported by bioluminescence imaging (Figure 5F-M, Figure 5—supplement 1B-C, p<0.01) and necropsy data (Figure 5I-J, N-O, p<0.01). Unlike MYF5 knockdown in Rh18, MYOD knockdown cells continued to grow albeit at reduced levels, suggesting additional mechanisms may contribute to growth in these cells. This difference is appropriately noted.

results.result: ChIP-seq analysis revealed that MYF5 and MYOD bind common DNA regulatory elements in human RMS, with 86% of commonly bound regions in enhancers (H3K27ac+), enriched for genes regulating cell cycle and myogenic cell fate.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C77-C78 are supported by ChIP-seq analysis (Figure 6A-C). The analysis appropriately uses H3K27ac to define enhancers and GREAT for gene ontology analysis. However, the ChIP-seq compares different cell lines (MYF5 in Rh18 vs MYOD in RD), which is a limitation but reasonable given mutual exclusivity. Binomial p<1×10⁻⁹ for GO terms is highly significant.

results.result: MYF5 and MYOD regulate transcription of genes controlling muscle development (Myogenin, CDH15) and cell cycle progression (CCND2), with downregulation observed following knockdown at 48-72hr.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C12, C79-C80, and C92 are supported by qRT-PCR data (Figure 6E) and ChIP-seq signal tracks (Figure 6D, Figure 6—supplement 1B). The functional validation of ChIP-seq targets strengthens the mechanistic model. Citation to Conerly et al. 2016 for myoblast regulation provides appropriate context. Statistical significance is shown for knockdown effects.

results.result: CCND2, a CDK4/6-associated cyclin amplified in RMS and required for proliferation, is a predicted direct target of MYF5/MYOD binding, with zebrafish ccnd2a showing trend toward higher expression in mylpfa:myf5 ERMS.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C84 are well-supported by citations. However, C81 shows only a trend (not statistically significant) in zebrafish ccnd2a expression (Figure 6—supplement 2). While the human data for CCND2 regulation is clear (C80), the zebrafish correlation is suggestive but not definitive. The connection between MYF5/MYOD and CCND2 regulation is supported but would benefit from additional validation.

results.result: TPCs drive tumor growth and relapse, have been identified in zebrafish and human RMS, with only Sonic-Hedgehog and WNT/β-catenin pathways previously shown to regulate TPC function in RMS subsets.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C15, C25-C26 establish background on TPCs in RMS. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. This provides context for the novelty of identifying MRF regulation of TPC function.

results.result: MYF5 and MYOD act redundantly in muscle development across species (mouse, zebrafish, Drosophila, Xenopus) and are required for satellite cell self-renewal, though recent work shows individual roles for each factor in specific muscle progenitor subsets.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C91 provide important biological context from developmental biology literature. All claims are supported by appropriate citations. This background establishes the biological plausibility of MRF roles in RMS and highlights the novelty of finding mutual exclusivity in cancer versus co-expression in development.

results.result: The CCND2 complex is required for myoblast proliferation and RMS growth, is highly expressed in primary human RMS, and is amplified in subsets of human and zebrafish RMS.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C94 are supported by citations to Chen et al. 2013a, Saab et al. 2006, and Webster and Fan 2013. This establishes CCND2 as a relevant downstream target of MRF regulation with known importance in RMS biology.
